messages.subject: Question: recapture as a function of a covariate, multistate model
messages.subject_clean: Question: recapture as a function of a covariate, multistate model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I am trying to model a multistate model where I aim to model recapture as a function of a covariate, and after some work a few questions have come to my mind.

Mine is a particular case of a multistate analysis in which the individual can be alive at two different states and dead at two different states too.

States
1 - Alive1
2 - Alive2
3 - Dead1
4 -  Dead2
5 - Long-dead (absorbing state)

All individuals enter the population at state 1 and at some points of their lives might or might not transition to state 2, from which they cannot go back to state 1 anymore. The thing here is, the probabilities of encounter (p) of individuals at state Alive1 and Alive2 are expected to differ so much, and have to be modelled differently. p(Alive1) is easy to model as a constant probability, but I'd like to model p(Alive2) using a linear relationship that depends on a covariate.

for(i in 1:num.inds){
pA2[i] <- mu + beta*x[i]
}

observation matrix:

obs[2,2,i,t] <- pA2[i]

In my case, the covariate "x" can only be quantified if the individual is actually observed at state 2 at least once. Therefore, the vector "x" that provides covariate values is a combination of NAs for those individuals which have not been observed at state 2 and exact values for those observed at state 2.

When trying to run my model parameterized as explained, it will end up crashing. The output complains about those elements in vector "x" filled with "NAs". I guess this makes sense as when the model assigns a transition 1 -> 2 to an individual whose fate is uncertain at any iteration, the recapture formula ends up being pA2[i] <- mu + beta*NA, which ultimately causes the crash.

My aim is to have a model in which we can estimate recapture probability pA2[i] as a function of the covariate, based on the data available. Do you guys have any idea on how to formulate this in a multistate model?

Please let me know if you need any more info, I'll be glad to provide it!  Any ideas or suggestions are welcome.

Have a nice week,

Jaume

messages.subject: Posterior predictive checks in hidden Markov models
messages.subject_clean: Posterior predictive checks in hidden Markov models
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm currently working on some posterior predictive checks of a multistate (2 alive states + 1 dead state) CMR model. In a nutshell, my likelihoods are as follows:

latent states z:
z[i,t,m] ~ dcat(omega[z[i,t-1,m], z[i,t,m], i, t, m])
observed states y:
y[i,t,m] ~ dcat(z[i,t,m], 1:3, i, t, m])

Now, I know we generate new replicate datasets like so:
y.new <http://y.new>[i,t,m] ~ dcat(theta[z[i,t,m], 1:3, i, t, m])

But do I also generate new latent states like this?
z.new <http://z.new>[i,t,m] ~ dcat(omega[z[i,t-1,m], z[i,t,m], i, t, m])

I think I read somewhere in the AHM books that you can't do it for latent states. But would this posterior predictive check be only on the observation part of the model? Because I think one's expected values would be:
theta[z[i,t,m], 1:3, i, t, m],

which is conditional on the latent states z which are only estimated once (from the data).

Looking forward to some insight on this!

Kind regards,
Matt

messages.subject_clean: Question: recapture as a function of a covariate, multistate model
messages.body_plain:
Hey Jaume,

Good question. I've recently had a similar problem and spent a lot of time thinking about this. One way of thinking that I got from Daniel Turek at the NIMBLE team is that when a covariate value is 0, beta*0 is also 0 and thus that covariate value does not contribute to the value of the coefficient. In his words:

"If you want it to ignore the beta and x[i] contribution to the mean, for these NA values of x[i], then you could instead specify the x[i] which are NA to instead have a value of 0, and thus beta * x[i] = beta * 0 = 0, and the model would "ignore" these (formerly) NA values of x[i], and they would not affect the mean of y[i], and they also wouldn't affect the inferences for beta."

Alternatively, you could impute missing covariates for individuals not observed from the distribution of the observed values. For instance, if it's something like temperature, you can impute missing values from N(temp_mu, temp_sd) of the observed covariate values. You could of course make this imputation more complex. For instance, I recently imputed missing disease infection loads from such a normal distribution that also included seasonal effects of temperature and rainfall–known to affect infection dynamics–and random individual effects (as some individuals were perhaps more likely to be infected than others).

Btw, the imputation of loads vs. replacing the NAs with 0s had negligible impact on the coefficient I was interested in! I think both methods can be justified.

Cheers,
Matt

messages.subject: Estimating abundance in the presence of transients using multi-state models
messages.subject_clean: Estimating abundance in the presence of transients using multi-state models
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have a long-term data set (77 capture occasions over a 35-year period) on tropical birds for which I am trying to estimate abundance. However, we have a substantial number of transients for each study species represented by 63-80% of capture occasions containing only a single capture (no recapture). I thought it may be possible to treat this as a multi-state/multi-event problem based on a combination of the multi-state parameterization of the Jolly-Seber model from Kery and Schaub (2012) with the multi-event transience models of Genovart and Paradel (2019). This approach has five states: Available-Resident, Unavailable-Resident, Available-Transient, Unavailable-Transient, Dead. Transition probabilities from Unavailable to Available states represent entry probabilities and Available-Transients allows immediately transition to the Dead state. Abundance would be calculated by summing across rows in the latent state matrix, z.

I have simulated some data under this design (see script below). However, when I run this model through JAGS I almost always get an error message: “Error in node y[1,5]; Node inconsistent with parents”. This error (almost) always refers to the first capture of the first individual. When the model does run, parameter estimates are highly biased.

I really like the conceptual approach of this multi-event framework but how does one define initial values with three unobservable states? Is this even possible? I was also wondering if there could be issues with identifiability in a multi-event model like this?

Thanks for any advice or suggestions! If someone knows of another approach for estimating abundance in open-populations in the presence of transients with a Jolly-Seber type of sampling design, please let me know!

Thanks,

Javan

R script for simulating data and (trying to!) fit the multi-event model

library(jagsUI)

set.seed(9876)

phi <- 0.5 # Resident survival

p <- 1 # Resident recapture probability

gamma <- 0.1 # Resident entry probability

eps <- 0.1 # Transient entry probability

tau <- 0.7 # Probability of being a transient

N <- 400 # Super-population size

int <- rep(c(4/12,8/12),((13-1)/2)) # Interval lengths between capture occasions

# State-transition parameters

UR <- c(1-gamma,gamma,0,0,0) # State 1, Resident-Unavailable

ARA <- c(0,phi,0,0,1-phi) # State 2, Resident-Available and alive

UT <- c(0,0,1-eps,eps,0) # State 3, Transient-Unavailable

AT <- c(0,0,0,0,1) # State 4, Transient-Available and alive

D <- c(0,0,0,0,1) # State 5, Dead

Init <- c(1-tau,0,tau,0,0) # Resident or Transient, but still unavailable

# for capture

n.occasions <- length(int)+1

CH <- z <- matrix(NA, nrow = N, ncol = n.occasions)

init_state <- rep(NA, N)

# Simulate

for(i in 1:N){

  # Simulate individuals as unavailable residents or transients

  init_state[i] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,Init)==1)

  # Does the individual become available at t=1?

  if(init_state[i]==1) z[i,1] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,UR)==1)

  if(init_state[i]==3) z[i,1] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,UT)==1)

  # Simulate the observed events

  if(z[i,1]%in%c(2,4)) CH[i,1] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,c(p,1-p))==1)

  if(z[i,1]%in%c(1,3,5)) CH[i,1] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,c(0,1))==1)

  # min_t <- ifelse(ent.occ[i]+1>ncol(z),ncol(z),ent.occ[i]+1)

  for(t in 2:n.occasions){

    # if(is.na <http://is.na>(z[i,t-1])) next

    if(z[i,t-1]==1) z[i,t] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,UR)==1)

    if(z[i,t-1]==2) z[i,t] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,c(0,phi^int[t-1],0,0,(1-phi^int[t-1])))==1)

    if(z[i,t-1]==3) z[i,t] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,UT)==1)

    if(z[i,t-1]==4) z[i,t] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,AT)==1)

    if(z[i,t-1]==5) z[i,t] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,D)==1)

    if(z[i,t]>5) stop()

    # Simulate the observed events

    if(z[i,t]%in%c(2,4)) {

      CH[i,t] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,c(p,1-p))==1)

      if(CH[i,t]!=1) stop("Incorrect CH=1")

    }

    if(z[i,t]%in%c(1,3,5)){

      CH[i,t] <- which(rmultinom(1,1,c(0,1))==1)

      if(CH[i,t]!=2) stop("Incorrect CH=2")

    }

  }

}

# Replace NA's with 2's

if(sum(is.na <http://is.na>(CH))>0) CH[is.na <http://is.na>(CH)] <- 2

# Were any individuals never captured?

# If so, remove

if(length(which(apply(CH,1,min)==2))>0){

# Source the JAGS model

sink("JAGS_multi_event_transient_model.txt")

  # t = year

  # mean.phi: probability of survival (residents only)

  # mean.p: probability of recapture conditional upon being alive (residents and transients)

  # mean.gamma: entry probability (residents and transients)

  ### States (S):

  # 1 Unavailable residents

  # 2 Available residents

  # 3 Unavailable transients

  # 4 Available transients

  # 5 Dead

  ### Observations (O):

  # 1 seen

  # 2 not seen

  mean.p ~ dbeta(1,1) # dunif(0,1)

  mean.phi ~ dbeta(1,1) # dunif(0,1)

  mean.tau ~ dbeta(1,1) # dunif(0,1)

  mean.gamma ~ dbeta(1,1) # dunif(0,1)

  mean.eps <- mean.gamma # ~ dunif(0,1) # dbeta(1,1)

  for (i in 1:M){

    pinit[i,2] <- 0

    pinit[i,3] <- mean.tau

    pinit[i,4] <- 0

    pinit[i,5] <- 0

    # at t=1 capture occasion. Can only transition from state 1 or 3

    # into states 1, 2, 3, or 4.

    psfirst[1,i,2] <- mean.gamma

    psfirst[1,i,3] <- 0

    psfirst[1,i,4] <- 0

    psfirst[2,i,1] <- 0 # Alive residents available

    psfirst[2,i,2] <- 0 # State 2 is not permitted at this point

    psfirst[2,i,3] <- 0

    psfirst[2,i,4] <- 0

    psfirst[3,i,1] <- 0 # Alive transients unavailable

    psfirst[3,i,2] <- 0

    psfirst[3,i,3] <- 1-mean.eps

    psfirst[3,i,4] <- mean.eps

    psfirst[4,i,1] <- 0 # Alive transients available

    psfirst[4,i,2] <- 0 # State 4 is not permitted at this point

    psfirst[4,i,3] <- 0

    psfirst[4,i,4] <- 0

    psfirst[5,i,1] <- 0 # Dead

    psfirst[5,i,2] <- 0 # State 5 is not permitted at this point

    psfirst[5,i,3] <- 0

    psfirst[5,i,4] <- 0

      ps[1,i,t,2] <- mean.gamma

      ps[1,i,t,3] <- 0

      ps[1,i,t,4] <- 0

      ps[1,i,t,5] <- 0

      ps[2,i,t,1] <- 0 # Alive residents available

      ps[2,i,t,2] <- mean.phi^int[t]

      ps[2,i,t,3] <- 0

      ps[2,i,t,4] <- 0

      ps[2,i,t,5] <- 1-(mean.phi^int[t])

      ps[3,i,t,1] <- 0 # Alive transients unavailable

      ps[3,i,t,2] <- 0

      ps[3,i,t,3] <- 1-mean.eps

      ps[3,i,t,4] <- mean.eps

      ps[3,i,t,5] <- 0

      ps[4,i,t,1] <- 0 # Alive transients available

      ps[4,i,t,2] <- 0

      ps[4,i,t,3] <- 0

      ps[4,i,t,4] <- 0

      ps[4,i,t,5] <- 1

      ps[5,i,t,1] <- 0 # Dead

      ps[5,i,t,2] <- 0

      ps[5,i,t,3] <- 0

      ps[5,i,t,4] <- 0

      ps[5,i,t,5] <- 1

    }

    for(t in 1:n.occasions){

      # Define probabilities of O(t) given S(t)

      po[1,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[1,i,t,2] <- 1

      po[2,i,t,1] <- mean.p

      po[2,i,t,2] <- 1-mean.p

      po[3,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[3,i,t,2] <- 1

      po[4,i,t,1] <- mean.p

      po[4,i,t,2] <- 1-mean.p

      po[5,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[5,i,t,2] <- 1

    } #t

    # Is each individual resident or transient (all unavailable)?

    x[i] ~ dcat(pinit[i,])

    # Does this individual transition to the available population on the first occasion?

    z[i,1] ~ dcat(psfirst[x[i],i,])

      # Observation equation: draw O(t) given S(t)

    aliveTrans[i] <- sum(alT[i,])

)

                           n.thin = 1,n.chains = 1,parallel=F))

> Hi everyone,
>
> I have a long-term data set (77 capture occasions over a 35-year period) on tropical birds for which I am trying to estimate abundance. However, we have a substantial number of transients for each study species represented by 63-80% of capture occasions containing only a single capture (no recapture). I thought it may be possible to treat this as a multi-state/multi-event problem based on a combination of the multi-state parameterization of the Jolly-Seber model from Kery and Schaub (2012) with the multi-event transience models of Genovart and Paradel (2019). This approach has five states: Available-Resident, Unavailable-Resident, Available-Transient, Unavailable-Transient, Dead. Transition probabilities from Unavailable to Available states represent entry probabilities and Available-Transients allows immediately transition to the Dead state. Abundance would be calculated by summing across rows in the latent state matrix, z.
>
>
>
> I have simulated some data under this design (see script below). However, when I run this model through JAGS I almost always get an error message: “Error in node y[1,5]; Node inconsistent with parents”. This error (almost) always refers to the first capture of the first individual. When the model does run, parameter estimates are highly biased.
>
> I really like the conceptual approach of this multi-event framework but how does one define initial values with three unobservable states? Is this even possible? I was also wondering if there could be issues with identifiability in a multi-event model like this?
>
> Thanks for any advice or suggestions! If someone knows of another approach for estimating abundance in open-populations in the presence of transients with a Jolly-Seber type of sampling design, please let me know!
